Unit 1: Summary Post collaborative discussion

In my original post, I discussed how digitalisation is becoming increasingly important for immigration services. Although digital systems can improve efficiency and reduce manual work, the problems with the UK Home Office Atlas system show that there are also risks. Technical problems can cause delays and additional work for employees, but can also have serious consequences for applicants who depend on decisions about their applications (Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration, 2024).

My peer's response made me look at this issue from a slightly different perspective. In my original post, I mainly focused on the consequences of technical problems, while my peer paid more attention to how these problems could have been prevented. For example, my peer suggested that new systems should be introduced more gradually, with better testing before they are fully implemented. I think this is an important point, because organisations often focus on the benefits of new technology, while the transition itself can also create problems. Research by Aguirre et al. (2019) also shows that careful planning, testing and choosing the right implementation approach are important when introducing new digital systems.

Another point raised by my peer was the importance of having clear procedures for situations where systems do not work. I already mentioned contingency procedures in my post, but I had not really considered what this means in practice. My peer mentioned regular backups, testing recovery procedures and training employees. I agree that these measures are important, because having a backup system does not necessarily mean that employees know how to use it when something goes wrong. Campbell et al. (2007) also emphasise the importance of preparing for situations where organisations become too dependent on technology.

The response also made me think differently about Industry 5.0. In my first post, I mainly connected the human-centred approach to the impact of digitalisation on applicants. However, I now realise that employees should also be part of this discussion. Pereira et al. (2025) emphasise the importance of involving workers in technological changes and supporting their development. I think this is also relevant for immigration departments, where employees need to be able to work with new systems and deal with technical problems.

Overall, my opinion has not really changed, but my peer's response helped me understand the issue better. I still believe that digitalisation can improve immigration services, but I now think that more attention should be paid to how new systems are introduced and how employees are prepared for possible problems.

Unit 3: Correlation and Regression

Covariance Pearson correlation (covariance_pearson_correlation.ipynb)

The original data shows a strong positive correlation (r = 0.888):

Increasing noise from 10 to 40 weakens correlation (r = 0.446):

Thus, random noise reduces Pearson correlation, demonstrating how greater data variability weakens the strength of a linear relationship.

Linear Regression (linear_regression.ipynb)

The original data shows a strong negative correlation (r = -0.759):

Changing one data point from 86 to 120 weakens the correlation (r = -0.074):

Thus, individual data points can significantly influence the regression line and weaken the relationship between variables.

Polynomial Regression (polynomial_regression.ipynb)

The original data shows a strong polynomial fit (R² = 0.943):

Changing one data point from 55 to 110 reduces the model fit (R² = 0.499):

Thus, individual observations can significantly affect polynomial regression accuracy and the shape of the fitted curve.

Unit 5: Jaccard Distance and Dissimilarity

In this exercise, I calculated Jaccard dissimilarity to compare the pathological test results of three individuals. First, I converted the asymmetric variables into binary values, assigning 1 to Y/P and 0 to N/A. Gender was excluded because it is a symmetric variable.

Using the Jaccard distance formula, I obtained the following results:

PairJaccard dissimilarity
Jack and Mary0.33
Jack and Jim0.67
Jim and Mary0.75

The calculations ignore shared zero values and focus on differences between positive observations.

The results demonstrate that Jack and Mary have the greatest similarity, while Jim and Mary have the greatest dissimilarity.

Unit 8: Summary Post collaborative discussion

In my first post, I argued that AI writers can be useful, especially for administrative tasks, but that their value depends on what we ask them to write. I also argued that the person using AI should remain responsible for the final text. After reading Dzemal’s and Patrick’s responses, I still agree with this, although I think I underestimated how difficult that responsibility can be in practice.

Dzemal made a point that I had not really considered. Because AI writes in such a confident and professional way, people may be less likely to question what it says. This is a problem, because a well-written answer can still contain incorrect information. Shao (2025) discusses how AI-generated inaccuracies can appear convincing. I originally suggested that people should check the output, but I now think this is easier said than done.

I also found Dzemal’s comment about academic writing relevant. I mainly discussed how AI can save time with drafts and summaries. However, when students use AI to do too much of the writing, they may also miss part of the learning process. Lee et al. (2025) found an association between higher confidence in AI and less critical thinking among knowledge workers. Although this research was not specifically about students, I think the concern also applies to academic writing.

Patrick asked who should actually be responsible for an AI-generated text. In my view, that responsibility remains with the person submitting it. Checking should therefore mean verifying important claims and sources, not only correcting sentences that sound strange.

My view on creative writing has stayed much the same. AI can help with ideas, but Doshi and Hauser (2024) found that AI-assisted stories became more similar to each other. Overall, I still see AI mainly as a tool to support writing, rather than something that should take over the process.

References

Doshi, A.R. and Hauser, O.P. (2024) 'Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content', Science Advances, 10(28), article eadn5290. Available at: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11244532/ (Accessed: 17 October 2026).

Lee, H.P., Sarkar, A., Tankelevitch, L., Drosos, I., Rintel, S., Banks, R. and Wilson, N. (2025) 'The impact of generative AI on critical thinking: Self-reported reductions in cognitive effort and confidence effects from a survey of knowledge workers', Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, article 1121, pp. 1–22. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713778 (Accessed: 17 October 2026).

Shao, A. (2025) 'New sources of inaccuracy? A conceptual framework for studying AI hallucinations', Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review, 6(4). Available at: https://doi.org/10.37016/mr-2020-182 (Accessed: 17 October 2026).
